clue.text: Change grip on the camera? I might

definitions.text: Change grip on the camera? I might

indicators.note: to change something is to alter its make-up, so the letters of the following words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A camera operator muses that they might adjust the way they hold the camera.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: the person who might change grip on the camera is the one filming, and 'Change' tells you to rearrange the letters of the words before the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The director of photography is the film-crew member who handles and adjusts the camera.

clue.text: Fried potato Her Maj's put below top of pan full of beans

indicators.note: in a down entry, being put below something means coming after it

parts.note: a chip is a fried potato

indicators.note: the top of a word in a down clue is its first letter

parts.note: ER, Elizabeth Regina, stands for Her Majesty

explanation.surface: A cook places a chip beneath the Queen's portion on a pan full of beans.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fried potato' and 'beans' suggest a kitchen; the definition is the idiom at the end. 'put below' places ER after the P from 'top of pan'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being full of beans is an idiom for lively and cheerful, a synonym for chirpy and bright.

clue.text: Dig uncovered housing close to Barking

indicators.note: one word housing another holds it inside

parts.note: uncovered means naked, nude

indicators.note: the close of a word is its last letter

explanation.surface: Someone digs on uncovered ground near Barking, a district of east London.
explanation.walkthrough: 'housing' puts G, the last letter of 'Barking', inside NUDE. Barking is a district of east London.
explanation.definitionFit: A dig in the ribs is a nudge, a poke with the elbow.

clue.text: Friend bringing friend around plot

indicators.note: the first friend goes around the second, holding it inside

parts.note: a mate is a friend
china is Cockney rhyming slang for mate, from china plate

explanation.surface: One friend brings another friend round to discuss a plot.
explanation.walkthrough: The second friend comes from Cockney rhyming slang, 'china plate' rhyming with mate. 'around' puts the first friend round the second.
explanation.definitionFit: To plot as a verb is to scheme or conspire, which is what this verb means.

clue.text: Carry books into Travelodge on vacation

indicators.note: the books go into the remaining letters
a word on vacation has been emptied, leaving only its outside letters

parts.note: OT is the Old Testament, books of the Bible

explanation.surface: A holidaymaker carries books into a Travelodge, a British budget hotel chain.
explanation.walkthrough: Travelodge is a British budget hotel chain; 'on vacation' empties it to its outer letters, and 'into' puts the books inside.
explanation.definitionFit: To carry a bag around is to lug or haul it, an informal verb sense.

clue.text: Group of troops army leave in unstable Saigon

indicators.note: the leave goes inside the rearranged city
something unstable is shaken about, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: R and R, rest and recreation, is military leave

explanation.surface: Troops on leave in a volatile wartime Saigon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unstable' rearranges the city to GAISON, and 'in' puts the leave inside it; R and R is rest and recreation.
explanation.definitionFit: A body of soldiers stationed to defend a town or fort is called this.

clue.text: Liberal involved in first-class defence

indicators.note: one piece involved in another is wrapped up inside it

parts.note: A1 (here AI) means first-class

explanation.surface: A Liberal politician mounts a first-rate defence.
explanation.walkthrough: First-class is A1, with the figure one read as the letter I; 'involved in' puts the Liberal inside.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspect's claim to have been elsewhere at the time is a defence against a charge.

clue.text: Condition rather posh boards dislike

indicators.note: letters that board a word climb inside it

parts.note: to hate is to dislike strongly
a bit means rather, somewhat
U means upper-class, posh

explanation.surface: Rather posh boarding schools are disliked by their pupils.
explanation.walkthrough: U as posh comes from the old 'U and non-U' labels for upper-class usage. 'boards' puts the posh pieces inside the dislike. 'Condition' is a verb here.
explanation.definitionFit: To condition someone is to accustom them through repetition, to make something second nature.

clue.text: Book about vacuous vicar up in Ely?

parts.note: re means about, concerning

indicators.note: the vicar's letters sit inside the bishop's seat

parts.note: Ely is a cathedral city, so an example of a see, a bishop's seat; the question mark flags the example

indicators.note: in a down clue going up reads the letters backwards
a vacuous word is empty, leaving its outside letters

explanation.surface: A book about a vacant-minded vicar, set in the cathedral city of Ely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'vacuous' empties 'vicar' to its outer letters, 'up' turns them round, and 'in' puts them inside the bishop's seat. Ely is a cathedral city in Cambridgeshire.
explanation.definitionFit: To book a table or a seat is to set it aside ahead of time.

clue.text: Charge men protecting a flasher

indicators.note: the outer letters protect what sits within them

parts.note: to indict is to formally charge
OR, other ranks, means enlisted men

explanation.surface: Police charge the men shielding an indecent exposer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'protecting' places A inside INDICTOR. 'flasher' looks like the man in the dock; it is the winking light on a car.
explanation.definitionFit: A car's flashing turn signal is its blinker, the light that shows which way it will turn.

clue.text: Bigwig bossing around Africans

indicators.note: the letters are lying around within the two words, spanning them

explanation.surface: An important figure bosses people about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'around' signals letters sitting within 'Bigwig bossing'.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nigerian ethnic people, one of the largest groups in West Africa.

clue.text: Abstract, but accurate without end

indicators.note: a word without its end loses its final letter

parts.note: precise means accurate

explanation.surface: An abstract that is concise but incomplete.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without end' drops the final E from PRECISE.
explanation.definitionFit: An abstract of a paper is a short summary of its main points.

clue.text: Sibling nurses at home on the left

indicators.note: to nurse is to hold close, so one word cradles another inside it

parts.note: a sister is a sibling
in means at home

explanation.surface: A sister nurses relatives at home on the left of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'nurses' looks like a noun about the sister's job; it is the verb that cradles 'at home' inside the sibling.
explanation.definitionFit: In heraldry and Latin the word means left-hand, the side of the bearer's left.

clue.text: Badly organised queen with a grand name

parts.note: R, regina, stands for queen
G is short for grand, a thousand
a tag is a name or label

explanation.surface: A queen with a grand title runs a shambolic court.
explanation.definitionFit: A disorganised, motley crowd is described as this, untidy and mixed.

clue.text: A regiment prepared to shoot?

indicators.note: something prepared is made ready, its parts reworked, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A regiment readies itself to open fire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shoot' reads as firing a gun; it is a plant putting out a shoot.
explanation.definitionFit: A seed that sprouts puts out a shoot; the verb means to begin growing.

clue.text: Novel storage unit in Spooner's kitchen?

indicators.note: Spooner swapped the opening sounds of words, so the two words of the phrase swap their first letters

parts.note: a kitchen is jokingly a cook base, the place where the cook works; this supplies the first word of that phrase
the second word of the whimsical phrase for a kitchen, the home ground or base of the cook

explanation.surface: A new storage unit for the kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'kitchen?' gives COOK BASE; swapping the first letters gives the answer. 'Novel' is not 'new' but a book stored there.
explanation.definitionFit: Shelving for books holds novels, so it is a storage unit for them.

clue.text: Erudition present in grand, abridged sort of book

parts.note: K, a thousand, is slang for a grand
now means the present

indicators.note: an abridged word is cut short, losing its last letter

parts.note: a ledger is a book of accounts

explanation.surface: Learning is presented in a grand, shortened book.
explanation.walkthrough: 'abridged' cuts LEDGER to LEDGE; 'in' just joins the pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Erudition is deep learning, the sum of what a scholar knows.

clue.text: Drink rum drinks in northern church

indicators.note: a word that drinks letters takes them in

parts.note: rum means odd, queer

explanation.surface: Someone drinks rum in a church in the north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rum' looks like the spirit; it is the old adjective meaning strange. 'drinks' takes the northern church inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: Something drunk to slake thirst is informally called this.

clue.text: Doctor turning water into Spar wine

indicators.note: these letters go into the boxing word

parts.note: to spar is to box

indicators.note: turning makes the doctor's letters read backwards

parts.note: eau is French for water

explanation.surface: A doctor performs a miracle, turning water into wine at the Spar, a convenience-store chain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turning' looks like turning water into wine; it reverses the doctor. Spar is a convenience-store chain, but here it means box; 'into' puts the rest inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Claret and other wines come from the French region and city around this port.

clue.text: Disapproving sounds heard in court session

indicators.note: heard tells you to take how the words sound when spoken

parts.note: boos are noises of disapproval
to be up before a judge is to be in court

explanation.surface: Jeers ring out during a court sitting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'session' sounds legal; it is a drinking session.
explanation.definitionFit: A session is a bout of heavy drinking, a binge.

clue.text: Not smiling, perhaps having chewed up lemons

indicators.note: something chewed up is mangled, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Anyone who has just chewed lemons would not be smiling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' marks the definition as one example of a grave face.
explanation.definitionFit: A grave, serious expression is one that is not smiling.

clue.text: Conk cleaner on flipping head for showing awful rage

indicators.note: flipping a word turns it over, so its letters read backwards
the head of a word is its first letter
awful suggests a mess, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone flipping out in a fit of rage gets told to wipe their nose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' turns 'on' into NO; 'awful' rearranges RAGE to ERAG. Conk is British slang for nose.
explanation.definitionFit: A handkerchief is slangily called this, a cloth for wiping the nose.

clue.text: Excluding love, university can start to grate

parts.note: O is love, zero in tennis
MIT is the Massachusetts Institute of Technology
a tin is a can

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: Leaving out love, a university can begin to irritate.
explanation.walkthrough: 'can' looks like a verb; it is a tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Leaving something out is excluding it.

clue.text: Very entertaining European elders?

definitions.note: elders are examples of a kind of tree; the question mark marks the example and the definition is plural

indicators.note: a host entertaining a guest has them inside

parts.note: tres is French for very

explanation.surface: Older Europeans are very amusing company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'elders' suggests older people; with the question mark it means elder bushes.
explanation.definitionFit: The elder is a flowering shrub or small woody plant, so elders are examples.

clue.text: Enquires after empty fuel bottles

indicators.note: the enquiring word comes after the emptied one
an empty word has its insides removed, leaving its outer letters

parts.note: asks means enquires

explanation.surface: Someone asks after the empty fuel bottles.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bottles' looks like a verb but is the definition, plural noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Hip flasks and vacuum flasks are kinds of bottle.

clue.text: Short tailor one needles

indicators.note: a short word loses its last letter

parts.note: to style is to tailor or fashion
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A short tailor uses a needle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'needles' looks like a tailor's tool; it is the record-player needle.
explanation.definitionFit: Record-player needles and engraving points are both called by this plural.

clue.text: Heading to Japan, one's to bring in black sails

indicators.note: the heading of a word is its first letter
one piece brings in another, holding it inside

parts.note: one's is one is, I IS
B is short for black, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A ship heading for Japan brings in black sails.
explanation.definitionFit: Triangular foresails on a boat are called this.

clue.text: Skirt promotion held by Adam's missus

indicators.note: the promotion is held inside the wife's name

parts.note: Eve was Adam's wife in Genesis
an ad is a promotion, an advertisement

explanation.surface: Eve wears a skirt in a fashion advert.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Skirt' looks like the garment; it is the verb meaning go round, avoid.
explanation.definitionFit: To skirt an issue is to dodge or sidestep it.

clue.text: Hire yard out by river for a Barnet setter?

definitions.note: Barnet is Cockney rhyming slang for hair (Barnet Fair), so something that sets a person's locks

indicators.note: out means not in order, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Hiring a yard beside a river as a base for a setter (a gun dog) from Barnet in north London.
explanation.walkthrough: Barnet is a north London borough, but in Cockney rhyming slang 'Barnet Fair' means hair. 'out' rearranges HIRE YARD.
explanation.definitionFit: A salon device blows warm air to dry and set the hair.

clue.text: Request right to visit royal for fun?

definitions.note: describes hunting for enjoyment, an adjective phrase

parts.note: a plea is a request
sure means right, certainly
to see someone is to visit them
a king is a royal

explanation.surface: Someone asks permission to visit a monarch just for fun.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for fun?' is a cryptic stab at the definition: someone after fun is chasing enjoyment.
explanation.definitionFit: A hedonist is driven by enjoyment, always chasing a good time.
